asDecan.p: Each sign gets cut into three slices of ten degrees, called decans, and every slice has a ruling planet and a small card of its own. Your Sun falls somewhere between ten and nineteen degrees of Scorpio, the middle slice, and the Golden Dawn hands that stretch to the Sun. So your Sun is sitting in a patch of sky the Sun itself looks after, which I always find a nice detail. It has no special dignity in Scorpio, mind you. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, and it takes on the colour of Mars, the sign's old ruler, and Pluto, the modern one. The middle of a sign is where it's settled and at full strength. The Five of Cups before you belongs to Mars and is somebody staring at spilt cups. The Seven after you belongs to Venus and is all daydreams and options. Yours is the one where some warmth gets down into the deep water. Death is still your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You keep things. There's a shoebox, or a drawer, or a folder on your phone, with the birthday card from 2009 and a voice message from your nan you've never been able to delete. At a family dinner you're the one who brings up the caravan holiday where the tent flooded, and you remember who was sulking and why. You remember what someone ordered on your first date with them, years later, and it slightly unnerves them. When a message from an old friend sits unanswered for a week you notice, and you don't say anything, but you notice. And a Sunday with nothing planned has a way of turning into three hours of old photos, which ends with you messaging somebody from Year 8 to ask if they remember that teacher.

The gift people don't expect from a Scorpio is repair. Plenty of this sign cuts people off and never looks back, and you can do that too, but the Sun in this slice gives you a way back in that the other two decans don't have. You're the one who sends the message to the friend you fell out with at nineteen, fifteen years on, and somehow it lands, because you remembered the good bits accurately and said so. Families use you for this without quite realising. When two siblings haven't spoken since the funeral, it's usually someone like you who rings both of them. You can go back into an old hurt, look at it properly, and come out with something warm in your hands. That's rare, to be honest, and it's worth knowing you can do it.

The less obvious trouble is that you get attached to the version of people you met first. Your best friend from school moves to Perth, makes new friends, gets into trail running and starts talking differently, and some part of you takes it personally, as if she's walked out on the old her and on you with it. You won't say that. You'll just go a bit cool on the phone. The same thing happens with places, and with bands, and with the café that got renovated. There's also a quiet ledger under the generosity. You give a lot, and you give well, but you remember every bit of it, and if it isn't returned in kind you can let it sit for years before it comes out in one sharp sentence during an argument about something else entirely.

When things go wrong you go backwards first. Bad news, a loss, a week of being overlooked at work, and you're on the couch with the film you watched at twelve, eating whatever your mum used to make when you were sick. That's fine for a night or two. By the end of the week it's usually gone into digging. You're reading old messages at one in the morning looking for the moment it started going wrong, or you've contacted an ex who has nothing to do with any of it, because they knew you when things felt simpler. The people around you, the ones who are here, start to feel like they're standing outside a closed door. What actually helps is one person who's known you a long time, sitting with you in daylight, and one small job done in the present with your hands.

You love through shared history, and a relationship gets better for you the longer it runs. The inside jokes, the ticket stubs, the fact that they know which aunt not to mention. The thing worth watching is that familiarity can feel like chemistry to you. Someone laughs like your dad, or has the same quiet way your first love had, and you're halfway in before you've found out who they are. I see this a lot with the Sun in the middle of Scorpio, and it's not always a problem, but it's worth asking yourself early on whether you're responding to them or to someone they remind you of. Once you're committed, anniversaries matter more than you'll admit. A forgotten one hurts, and you'll say it's fine.

You do well anywhere that values memory and doesn't rush people. A lot of people with the Sun here end up in roles with long tenure, the family business, the school they went to, the hospital ward where they know every regular by name. Restoration work suits you, whether it's furniture, old houses, archives or people. Counselling that goes into childhood, early learning, aged care and heritage work all come up a lot in charts like this, as does the sort of client work where you remember the names of their kids. The snag is loyalty past its use-by date. You'll stay in a job for years because of a manager who left in 2019, telling yourself it's the same place. Every couple of years, ask honestly whether you'd apply for it again.

At twenty this slice is often already nostalgic, which surprises people. You're missing sixteen while you're still in your first share house, keeping every note and holding a couple of grudges very tightly. By the mid-thirties most people with the Sun here have learned the difference between keeping something and clinging to it, usually the hard way, after a friendship or a relationship that was only alive in memory. The box of keepsakes gets smaller and the few things in it matter more. The fifties tend to bring a softer version. You become the one who holds the family photos, patches up old rifts and takes younger people under your wing, and you're less bothered when someone changes on you, because you've changed a fair bit yourself.

Once a month, send one message to someone from an older part of your life. Name a specific thing you remember about them, the song they always put on or the way they drove, and don't ask for anything back or suggest catching up. Then, the same week, go through your keepsakes and give away or throw out one thing that only brings back weight. Keep the one next to it that still makes you smile.
